text: Grandpa Leo sat in his quiet kitchen with the tablet in front of him. Autumn had come, and he needed a warm coat. Last week he had ordered one online, but it turned out to be too small. 'Return coat,' he said to the tablet. The assistant understood that he wanted to send back the coat from last week's order. It opened the order and asked if he wanted his money back or a bigger size. 'Swap it,' said Leo. The assistant picked the next size up in the same blue color and set up the exchange. It printed a return label and told him the new coat would come in four days. Leo smiled. He put the old coat in the box and set it by the door, ready for the driver to pick up in the morning.

Mr. Okafor ran a small kitchen shop on Pine Street. Between customers, he said to his phone, 'Please call my supplier and read me my new messages.' The assistant understood two things: it should call the supplier saved in his contacts, and it should read out his unread messages. It started the call, and while the phone rang, it read two messages aloud. One was from a polite customer asking if the red blender was back in stock. The other was about a late delivery. Then the supplier picked up, and the assistant turned on the speaker. Soon a bell rang at the front door, so Mr. Okafor paused the call and the messages. When the customer left, he told the phone to resume, and it read the rest of the messages. He wrote the new delivery day on a notepad.

They want to know what time their flight leaves.
When do I take off?
Departure time?
What time is my flight tomorrow?
Is my flight earlier or later than half past nine?
I got my ticket in a big sale, so can you check when the plane leaves?
I'm putting the grill away before I go, so how many hours do I have until takeoff?
Could you please tell me the departure time? I have a large bag to check, and I want to leave home early enough.

A contact is a small card in your phone with a name, a phone number, and sometimes an address or a birthday. It is for finding people fast, so you never have to remember every number. People change their contacts all the time. They add a new friend, fix a wrong number, or add a birthday so the phone can remind them. When Tom met a new neighbor named Honey Park, he said, 'Add Honey to my contacts with this number.' Later he said, 'Change her number to the new one' and 'Put her birthday on March ninth.' If you point out a wrong number, you can say, 'That one is old, fix it.' You can also say 'remove' when someone is no longer needed. Most people are glad when the phone just does it.

name: share_daily_agenda
does: Folds the notes people send into one agenda for the day and shares it with everyone in the meeting.
inputs: the meeting, and who should get the agenda
people say:
- Send everyone what we're talking about today.
- Can you email the plan for the meeting to the team?
- The new artist on our team hasn't seen the list of topics yet, can she get it?
- Put all our notes together and show them to the group.
- Who is going to talk about what at ten o'clock? Send it around.

Person: I want to start a model of an old train station. Can you find me a plan?
Assistant: Of course. Would you like a big model or a small one?
Person: A small one. I am busy with other projects, so something easy.
Assistant: Do you want a kit made of wood blocks or of paper?
Person: Wood blocks, please. About twenty-five pieces.
Assistant: I found a wooden station kit with twenty-six blocks. Should I put it on your shopping list?
Person: Yes, please. Can you also bake the glue so it dries faster?
Assistant: I'm sorry, I can't do that. I can set a timer for the drying time, though.
Person: Lovely idea. Set it for two hours.
Assistant: Done. I will tell you when two hours are up.

Person: wifi is slwo, make it faster
Assistant: I can restart the router for you. Do you want me to do it now?
Person: not yet. my pair of coworkers are on a call
Assistant: Okay. When should I restart it?
Person: after lunch
Assistant: What exact time should I use?
Person: 1:30
Assistant: Done. The router will restart at 1:30, and it will beep once when it is back on.

They want to know how long the drive will take.
How long to get there?
Drive time to the school?
How many minutes is the trip to my aunt's house?
Is the highway faster than the back roads, or about the same?
I have to drop off the kid and I'm hanging on to a tight schedule, so how long will the drive take?
Will it take more than half an hour to reach the dry cleaner?
Could you please tell me how much time I should plan for the drive downtown?

Rosa was cooking dinner when her phone buzzed on the counter. Her hands were covered in flour, so she could not type anything. 'Who called me?' she asked the phone. The assistant said her sister had called twice and left a voicemail. 'Don't play it on the speaker,' said Rosa. 'I do not want the whole kitchen to hear.' A spider ran across the wall, and Rosa jumped, but she stayed calm. The assistant played the voicemail quietly into her ear. Her sister said her own dinner was already cooked and asked if Rosa wanted to come over. Rosa said, 'Call her back, but don't leave a message if she doesn't answer.' The assistant dialed, and when her sister picked up, Rosa said she would come at six.

name: resume_playback
does: Finds the spot where you stopped a podcast or audiobook and starts playing again from there.
inputs: the podcast or book, if there is more than one
people say:
- Where did I stop?
- I got a call in the middle of the chapter, so take me back to it.
- Keep going from where I left off in my book.
- Pick up the show about how to grill fish where it ended.
- I'm a patient listener, but I forgot the spot, so find it for me.

Mrs. Hale, a retired teacher, burned her hand on a hot pan on a warm day in June. She had just finished eating lunch and was washing up. 'Excuse me, could you please tell me what to do for a small burn on my hand? I want to be careful, because my grandchildren are visiting this afternoon and I do not want to make it worse,' she said to her phone. The assistant understood that she had a small burn and wanted safe first aid steps. It told her to hold her hand under cool running water for ten minutes, not to use ice or butter, and to cover the burn loosely with a clean cloth. It also said that if the burn blistered or hurt a lot, she should see a doctor. Mrs. Hale said thank you, and she was glad of the strong, clear advice.

Ben was late for his first class when he remembered the package he was waiting for. He pulled out his phone and typed fast: 'wher is my sugar order from monday'. The assistant understood that he wanted to know where his order of sugar from Monday was. It looked through his shopping account, found the order, and said the package was out for delivery and would arrive before five. Ben had a bad feeling that it was lost, because the shop had sent the wrong thing once before. But the assistant also said the driver was only three stops away. Ben let out a breath. He could chill now. He put his phone away, and the assistant promised to tell him as soon as the box arrived at his door.

They want the air conditioning to come on at a certain time.
Turn on the AC at six tomorrow evening.
Start cooling the house tomorrow at seven.
Can you make the bedroom cool by ten tonight?
Have the fan going when I get home at half past five.
I'd like the living room nice and cold when the guests come, around seven on Saturday.
It's going to be hot Friday morning, so help me out and get the cooling running by eight.
The weather is mild until noon, but after that please switch the cooling on.
Please make sure the apartment is cool before I walk in, because I'm back at noon on Monday.

name: set_dough_timer
does: Sets a timer for how long bread dough should rise, then tells you when it is time to shape it or put it in the oven.
inputs: the kind of dough, and how warm the room is
people say:
- Tell me when my bread has risen enough.
- How long should I let this dough sit?
- My dough is on the couch under a blanket, so call me when it has doubled.
- The dough looks rough and lumpy, how much longer should it rest?
- Remind me when to paint the loaf with egg before it goes in.

A shopping list is a short note of what you need to buy, so you don't forget things at the store. Many people keep one on their phone and put something on it whenever it runs out. When Sam saw the fridge was empty, he said, 'Put milk and eggs on my list.' Later he said, 'Take off the eggs, I found some' and 'I need two more bananas.' Some people take a picture of the fridge and ask the assistant what is missing. If a recipe is in cups and you want it in grams, you can ask the assistant to convert it. It is funny how often a list saves a second trip. People also say 'we're out of rice' or 'we need bread' to mean the same as 'add it to the list'.

Maya had just moved to the city, and her new building had a wall of small mailboxes. She did not know which one was hers, and she had no key yet. Standing in the hall, she said to her phone, 'I wonder if my mom's parcel ever found my new address.' The assistant understood that she wanted to know where the parcel was. It found the tracking number in her email and said the package had been taken to the post office on Elm Street, in the back of the building next to the bank, after one failed delivery. It would be held for five days. Maya said she could not afford to miss it again, so the assistant set a reminder to pick it up tomorrow at nine. It also saved her new address in her account as her permanent one.

Walt never trusted gadgets. His daughter had put a voice assistant in his car, and he spoke to it as if it were deaf. 'Tell me where I parked and how much gas is left,' he shouted. The assistant understood two things: Walt wanted to know where his car was parked, and how much fuel was left in the tank. It said the car was on the third floor of the garage, near the elevator, and that the tank was a quarter full. Walt had to guess how far that would take him, so he asked, and the assistant said about sixty miles. In the glove box Walt found a parking slip with an hourly price on it. He told the assistant to remind him to pay before he left, and it said it would.

Dana woke up groggy and remembered the shelf she was building. She had lost the last screw. 'Order more screws, but not the big ones,' she mumbled to the speaker by her bed. The assistant understood that she wanted small screws, not large. It looked at her past orders and found a pack of small screws at the hardware store she had used before. It said the pack of fifty cost four dollars. 'And don't use the rush shipping,' Dana said, rubbing her eyes. The assistant chose normal shipping and said the order would follow the usual schedule and arrive on Thursday. Dana thanked it, turned over, and went back to sleep.

Priya was packing boxes while her two kids zoomed around the empty living room. Outside it was a snowy day, and the wind rattled the old window. 'The movers come tomorrow, and I wonder who tells the gas company where we're going,' she said to her phone. The assistant understood that she needed to move her utilities to the new house. It added a task to her list, 'Tell the gas and power companies the new address,' and set a reminder for eight that evening. It also read out the phone number of the gas company so she could write it on the side of a box. Priya sighed, thanked it, and went back to taping the kitchen things.

Person: It's too bright in here. My eyes hurt.
Assistant: I can dim the lights. Which room are you in?
Person: The bedroom. I just got home and I want to sleep.
Assistant: Okay. Should I make them half as bright?
Person: Less than that. A quarter.
Assistant: Done. The bedroom light is at twenty-five percent.
Person: Thanks. The light in the broom closet is on too, and I don't want to spend the day with it glowing.
Assistant: I turned it off.
Person: Also, has the slow cooker finished? My stew should be cooked by now.
Assistant: I'm sorry, I can't check the slow cooker. I can only control the lights.

Person: Hello, could you please set a reminder for me? I just moved here, and I keep forgetting to call my mother on Sundays because she lives so far away.
Assistant: Of course. What time on Sunday should I remind you?
Person: She lives to the east, so there is a time difference. Five in the afternoon, please.
Assistant: Okay. I'll remind you every Sunday at five. What should the reminder be called?
Person: Please name it Call Mom.
Assistant: Done. The reminder Call Mom will ring every Sunday at five.
Person: Can you also tell me when she wakes up?
Assistant: Sorry, I can't know that. You could ask her what time works best.

Person: I need a hotel room for this weekend.
Assistant: Which city, and for how many nights?
Person: Denver, two nights. Wait, make it three. We decided to stay longer.
Assistant: Three nights in Denver. How many guests?
Person: Two adults and two kids. We need a big room.
Assistant: I found a family room with two beds. Do you want me to hold it?
Person: Yes, please. Is the hotel quiet? The volume of street noise matters because of my baby.
Assistant: I can't hear the street myself, but guests say the rooms at the back are quiet.
Person: Good. I'll click on the link you send and pay there.
Assistant: I just sent it to your phone.

name: warm_room_by_time
does: Heats one room to a chosen temperature at a chosen time, and can cancel the plan if you change your mind.
inputs: which room, how warm, and what time
people say:
- Get the south bedroom cozy by seven.
- I'm cold on the sofa, so warm up the living room.
- Heat the kitchen to twenty degrees at six in the morning.
- Never mind about tonight, cancel the heating plan.
- It's chilly in here, can you do something about it?

Leo was babysitting his baby cousin while his aunt was out. He was playing a game on his computer, trying to win a level, when the baby started to cry. He typed to the assistant, 'She hasn't eaten since noon and she's really loud.' The assistant understood that he wanted to know when the baby should eat. It checked the baby log in the family app and said that the last feeding was at noon. It said she usually eats every three hours, and the minimum wait between feeds was two hours, so it was time. Leo closed the game, warmed the bottle, and fed her. The assistant then noted the new feeding time in the log, so his aunt would see it when she came home.

Nia got home from the hospital at seven in the morning, tired and hungry. She ran the neighborhood group page, and she had promised to post a photo of the block party. 'Post my block party picture to the neighborhood group tomorrow at seven,' she said to the smart speaker, and then she yawned. The assistant understood that she wanted the photo posted later, not right now. It found the newest picture, which showed a plate of burnt sausages and a lot of smiling people, and it scheduled the post for seven the next morning. It asked if she wanted comments turned on, and she said yes. The assistant said the post was ready, and Nia went to bed.

Sam woke up on the sofa and heard rain on the roof. He felt small and sleepy. He had a job interview, but he had no idea what time it was or how the roads were. 'Traffic to downtown?' he mumbled to his phone. The assistant understood that he meant how heavy the traffic was on the way to downtown. It said there was an accident on the main road, and the drive would take forty minutes instead of twenty. 'Does that mean I'm late?' he asked. The assistant said that if he left in ten minutes he would still be on time. Sam jumped up, grabbed his coat, and ran for the door.

They want the pet feeder to give the dog his dinner.
Feed the dog.
It's time for the dog's dinner.
The dog is staring at his empty bowl.
Rex keeps pacing in front of the cupboard where his food is kept.
I don't want him to beg while I tidy the kitchen, so could you give him his food?
My dog hasn't had his dinner and it's getting late.
Please fill his bowl with one cup of food. He ate a few apple slices earlier, so it can be a small dinner.

name: check_pantry_stock
does: Looks at what is in the kitchen and counts how many of each thing is left.
inputs: the food or item to check, and where it is kept if you want
people say:
- How many eggs do we have?
- Are we out of rice?
- It's midnight and I want cereal, is there any milk left?
- Count the cans of soup in the cupboard.
- I only buy olive oil yearly, so do I still have some from the last time?

A focus timer is a way to work for a short time without distractions and then take a break. It is for people who find it hard to stay on one task. A common plan is twenty-five minutes of work and five minutes of rest. People often change the plan when it doesn't fit their day. A student might say, 'Make my work time longer,' or 'Make the break shorter.' A traveler waiting at the airport, with only a narrow gap before the gate opens, might say, 'Set a timer for ten minutes so I can answer my emails.' When the timer rings, you stand up, stretch, or charge your phone. Then you start the next round.

Mr. Ito, a retired teacher, kept his front hall tidy and his door always locked. One evening he sat down in his chair and could not remember if he had locked up. 'Is the front door locked?' he asked the speaker. The assistant said it was unlocked. 'Don't open it for anybody,' said Mr. Ito. 'I only want it locked.' The assistant locked the door and said it was done. Then he asked, 'Remind me to lock it every night at nine.' The assistant set the reminder. Mr. Ito felt a great amount of worry leave him. He thanked the speaker, picked up his book, and read until bedtime.

A birthday reminder is a note that tells you when someone's birthday is coming, so you can send a card or a gift on time. It is for people who don't want to forget. People add the date when they meet someone, and they change it if it was wrong. Someone might say, 'Remind me about Grandma's birthday a week before,' or 'Put Jake's birthday on June fourth.' When they need a gift idea, they say, 'What should I get a ten-year-old who loves to dance?' or 'Find a red scarf for my sister.' Some people sit down on a Sunday and put all the dates for the month into the phone. If a date changes, they just say, 'Move it to the fifth.'

Marta owned a small cafe and wanted to make pea soup for tomorrow at noon. Her recipe fed four people, but she needed to serve twelve. 'Make this pea soup recipe for twelve,' she told her phone. The assistant understood that she wanted every amount in the recipe multiplied by three. It read out the new list: nine cups of peas, three purple onions, and twelve cups of water. Then it told her the shopping would cost about fifteen dollars. Marta said that was fine, so the assistant put the new list in her notes and set a reminder to start cooking at nine tomorrow morning.

They want to know who is winning the game.
Who's ahead?
What's the score?
Is anyone beating me right now?
Tell me the points for each player.
I think my sister has more points than me, is that right?
I'm feeling sad because I keep losing, so could you tell me how far behind I am?
In our basket toss game, which team has more points?
Please check the score in the score book and tell me if the blue team is ahead, even by a little.

Carlos was busy at his shop when he remembered that his uncle took his medicine at noon. It weighed on his mind, because his uncle was old and often forgot. Carlos typed fast on his phone: 'call my uncel and remind him to take his pills'. The assistant understood that Carlos wanted it to call his uncle and tell him about his pills. It dialed the number saved as Uncle Rafael, and when he picked up, it said in a clear voice that it was time for his noon medicine. Then it told Carlos the call was done. Carlos was glad that the personal task had taken only a few seconds, and he went back to helping a customer.

Strength and sweetness are the two things people most often change about a drink. Coffee can be strong or weak, tea can be light or dark, and a smoothie can be thick or thin. Usually a person asks for one change at a time. They say, 'Make it stronger,' 'a bit sweeter,' or 'increase the sugar by one spoon.' If it is too much, they say 'less sweet' or 'make it half as strong.' A fancy cafe may offer many choices, but at home you can also ask for 'one more scoop of coffee' when you make a pot. A can of soda is sweet already, so some people add ice instead.

Person: Call Anna, please.
Assistant: I have two Annas, Anna Lee and Anna Brooks. Which one?
Person: Anna Lee. No, wait, I mean my sister, Anna Brooks.
Assistant: Calling Anna Brooks now.
Person: Oh dear, she is staying at a hotel, and it is late there. Should I wait?
Assistant: I can wait and call her in the morning, or I can leave her a message. Which do you want?
Person: Leave a message later. The light on my phone is flashing. What does that mean?
Assistant: It probably means you have a new voicemail. Do you want me to play it?
Person: Yes, please. My eyes are foggy today, so read it to me.
Assistant: Playing it now.

Joel ran out of the house with his bag, late for work. 'Set the pool heater to twenty-eight, I'm in a hurry,' he said to his phone as he locked the door. The assistant understood that he wanted the pool water to reach twenty-eight degrees. It scanned the pool app, saw that the water was only twenty degrees, and turned the heater on. It also checked the battery of the pool robot and told him that it was low. Joel said he would charge it tonight. The assistant noted that everything worked well, and it promised to tell him when the water reached the right heat. Joel hopped into his car and drove off.

Priti stumbled into her kitchen after a long shift, still wearing her earbuds. Her coffee was stale from the morning, but she was too tired to make more. She typed to her phone: 'read my new mesages and tell mom i will call after i sleep'. The assistant understood that she wanted two things: to hear her new texts, and to send a reply to her mom. It read three messages into her earbuds, one from her friend, one from her brother, and one from her mom. Then it sent a text to her mom that said Priti would call after she slept. Priti said thanks, put the phone down, and went to bed.

Greg sat at his desk before a meeting. In front of him was a list of costs for a new office tv. 'What is three hundred twenty plus one hundred eighty, and is that more than my five hundred dollar budget?' he asked his phone. The assistant understood that he wanted two numbers added together and then compared with his budget. It said the total was five hundred, which was exactly his budget, not more. Greg said that was perfect and asked the assistant to update the total in his notes. It did, and it added a line saying the budget was now used up. Greg nodded and walked to the meeting.

Person: book a table at the pasta place for frdiay
Assistant: Sure. What time, and how many people?
Person: 7 pm, four people
Assistant: Friday at seven for four. Do you want a table inside or outside?
Person: inside. last time our table wobbled because of a loose screw
Assistant: I'll add a note asking for a steady table. Anything else?
Person: can you get us a deep booth in the corner?
Assistant: I can ask, but I can't promise a booth. I'll send the request.
Person: ok. we can't afford anything fancy, so check that it's cheap
Assistant: The pasta place has main dishes from ten to fifteen dollars.

Tom closed his shop at six, tired after a long day. He sat on the sofa with a bowl of pea soup and picked up his phone. 'Show movies,' he said. The assistant understood that he wanted to see what films were on tonight. It listed three films at the cinema near him, with their times, and it also found a simple old comedy on his streaming app. Tom picked the comedy. The assistant connected his phone to the tv and started the film. Tom put his feet up, ate his soup, and laughed the whole way through.

Harold was not good with technology, and he did not trust his new smart lock. One evening he came home with a big painting in both arms and could not use his key. 'Open the front door,' he said. Nothing happened. He said it again, twice as loud as before. The assistant answered that it had not heard him well, because he was too far from the speaker. Harold took a deep breath and spoke more slowly. This time the door unlocked with a soft click, and the assistant said it was open. Harold's smile grew. He carried the painting inside, and he thought the new lock was perfect after all.

Person: My sister's birthday is next week and I have no idea what to get her.
Assistant: I can help with that. What does she like?
Person: She talks about her dream trip to Japan all the time.
Assistant: Nice. What is your budget?
Person: Under fifty dollars. I'm about to park at home, and I'm so tired.
Assistant: Then how about a Japan travel book? I found one for thirty-five dollars.
Person: Perfect. Can you wrap it and carry it upstairs to her apartment?
Assistant: I'm sorry, I can't carry things. I can order it with gift wrap and send it to her address.
Person: Do that, please.

They want a recipe changed to feed more people.
Make this recipe for eight.
Double it.
Scale the cake for twelve slices and give me a new shopping list.
Make it for six and tell me which cups and spoons I need.
I'm excited to cook for the whole family, so change the recipe to serve ten and tell me how much butter to use.
We have more guests than I thought, so please make it bigger.
Cut this in half and tell me the new baking time.
I nailed this cake last time, but only for four people, so please change it for nine. I want the glaze to shine, so change that too.

They want ideas for what to eat this week.
What's for dinner?
I have no idea what to cook this week.
It's snowy outside and I'm not going to the store, so what can I make with what I have?
My fridge is nearly empty and the week is long.
I'm tired of eating the same thing every night.
I'm trying to practice a better balance of vegetables and rice, so what should I cook?
Could you please plan five easy dinners for me, and think of something for my packed lunches?

Grandma Joy sat by the pool under a clear sky, with the sun shining brightly. But the water felt cold on her toes. 'Heat pool,' she said to the speaker. The assistant understood that she wanted the pool heater turned on. It turned on the electric heater and set it to the usual temperature of thirty degrees. It told her the water would take about two hours to warm up. Joy said that was fine, because she was in no hurry. She picked up her book and read in the sun. When the time was up, the assistant told her the pool was ready.

Luis was cooking dinner for the kids. He tasted the soup with one hand and held his phone in the other. The screen looked pale and he could hardly read it, so he asked the assistant to make it brighter. Then he said, 'Turn on do not disturb tonight at eight, and keep it on until tomorrow at seven.' The assistant understood that he wanted no calls or alerts during that time. It set the schedule and asked if it should filter out calls from family. Luis said yes, because his mother might call. The assistant allowed only family and said the quiet time was set. Luis put the phone down and called the kids to the table.

Nora waited at her desk. It was going to snow, and her flight to Chicago was at four. A silver suitcase stood beside her chair, and her boarding card was in her bag. 'Flight status?' she asked her phone. The assistant understood that she wanted to know how her flight was doing. It checked and said the flight was delayed by forty minutes, so the new departure was at 4:40 from gate B12. Nora sighed, but she was glad to know. She finished one more email, closed her laptop, and walked to the elevator with her suitcase.

Hana took out the recycling and noticed a smoky smell in the air from a fire far away. When she came back in, she said to her phone, 'Run the air purifier in the kids' room tomorrow at seven, and keep it on until they leave for school.' The assistant answered that it understood: it would turn on the purifier in the kids' room at seven tomorrow and turn it off at eight. It also asked if she wanted that every school day. Hana said yes, so the assistant made it a permanent schedule for weekdays. It then told her the air outside was poor today and suggested she keep the windows closed.

Ines was minding her shop on a cold afternoon, and the old radiator was clanking in the corner. Her son Lucas had a math worksheet, but she had forgotten the date. She typed quickly on her phone: 'when is lucas homewrk due'. The assistant understood that she wanted to know when Lucas's homework was due. It looked in the school app and said the math worksheet was due on Friday. Ines was relieved. Then the assistant told her about a funny note from the teacher on the page, which said Lucas had drawn a cat in the margin. Ines laughed, watered the plant by the door, and went back to her customers.
